extracted.intended_audience: patent practitioners, inventors, and law students
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for determining what kinds of subject-matter are patentable (machines, manufactures, compositions, arts), how to characterize a claimed subject (machine vs manufacture vs composition), and the unity/singularity required in a patent (when multiple improvements or machines may be joined or must be separate).

rubrics_metrics.name: Statutory classes of patentable subject-matter
rubrics_metrics.description: The statute enumerates classes of subjects held to be patentable: machinery (machines), manufactures (fabrics or substances made by the art or industry of man, not being machinery), compositions of matter, and arts (processes). The subject-matter of a patent should be one invention or discovery.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat a claimed invention as falling within one of these classes; the statutory language and the singular phrasing ('invention or discovery' not 'inventions or discoveries') indicate a patent should have a single subject-matter. Where classification is unclear, determine if the thing is a machine, a vendible manufacture, a composition, or an art (process of making).

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of 'manufacture'
rubrics_metrics.description: A 'manufacture' has been defined as 'something made by the hands of man' and more generally as 'any new combination of old materials, constituting a new result or production, in the form of a vendible article, not being machinery.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Focus on whether the claimed thing is a vendible article produced by combining materials into a new result; vendibility (marketable commodity) and the new result are key. Examples include medicines, stoves, telescopes; avoid classifying tools/parts used primarily as elements of machinery as 'manufactures' unless sold and used separately as merchantable commodities.

rubrics_metrics.name: Manufacture vs machine test
rubrics_metrics.description: If an article is produced and intended to be sold and used separately as a merchantable commodity and its merit lies in being a better article or produced more cheaply, it is a 'manufacture.' But if its merit appears only after incorporation with mechanism and it produces a new effect when combined with machinery, it is a 'machine' or an improvement of a machine.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When deciding how to claim, consider the article's intended sale/use and whether its inventive character is intrinsic (manufacture) or realized only when combined with machinery (machine). Range claims accordingly—classify under the one whose test the item satisfies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Composition of matter novelty test
rubrics_metrics.description: For compositions, 'the test of novelty must, of course, be, not whether the materials of which the composition is made, are new, but whether the combination is new.' Different proportions or combinations of known ingredients that produce a new composition can be patentable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate novelty by the combination and resulting composition, not merely the individual ingredients. If the article itself is not new but a new mode/process of producing it is discovered, the proper subject is the 'art' (process), not a 'composition of matter' patent for the article itself.

rubrics_metrics.name: Designs as patentable subjects and comparison to copyright
rubrics_metrics.description: New and original designs for manufactures, printing of fabrics, busts, statues, impressions or ornaments on articles, new shapes or configurations, and useful patterns/prints/pictures attached to articles are patentable (seven-year term). These patents occupy a middle ground between copyrights and patents.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Apply principles similar to identifying identity or colorable imitation in copyright when comparing designs; look for colorable imitation (not exact resemblance) to determine infringing similarity. Consider both form and device identity tests used for books/engravings.

rubrics_metrics.name: Unity (singularity) of the subject-matter requirement
rubrics_metrics.description: Acts require that the subject-matter of a patent should be one invention or discovery; where there are two distinct and independent inventions applicable to different objects and purposes they cannot be united in one patent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ask whether claimed items are distinct, independent inventions with no necessary connection or common purpose. If so, separate patents should be taken; inclusion of multiple unconnected inventions risks voiding the whole patent if part is not original.

rubrics_metrics.name: Unity test: the inventor's objective (common purpose)
rubrics_metrics.description: The object which the inventor proposes to accomplish is the main guide to determine whether his subject-matter is a unit. If several distinct inventions are brought together for a purpose which can only be effected by their union, that indicates unity. If the patent claims both the combination and the distinct purposes each invention can perform separately, multiple subject-matters are embraced.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Analyze the specification/claims to see whether the inventor treats the items as modes for achieving one object (supporting unity) or as separate inventions each serving independent purposes (pointing to multiplicity).

rubrics_metrics.name: Coverage of parts vs coverage of combination
rubrics_metrics.description: If the patentee describes several distinct and independent parts intended to be used in combination and is the first inventor of each, the patent covers the parts as well as the combination and the use of any one part by another is infringement. But if the patentee is not the inventor of the several things used in the combination and the combination itself is the true subject-matter, use of some of those things not amounting to the same combination is no infringement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Determine whether the patentee claims and invented each constituent part; where only the combination is his invention, infringement requires substantially the same combination. This affects claim drafting and enforcement strategy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Permissible joining of several improvements
rubrics_metrics.description: A patent may be taken for several improvements on the same machine, or for two machines invented by the patentee that conduce to the same common purpose and object (even if capable of distinct use), preserving unity. But a patent cannot be for two distinct machines designed for totally distinct and independent objects.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Where multiple improvements or alternative machines are all directed to one end (common purpose), they may be united in one patent; where they have totally different ends, separate patents are required. Consider the 'modes'/alternatives the specification teaches as a means to preserve unity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Specification accuracy and limitation to stated invention
rubrics_metrics.description: When a patentee in his specification states and sums up the particulars of his invention, and his patent covers them, he is confined to such summary; courts cannot reject the claim, and if anything included in that summary is not new the patent is void (even if that part is slight or unimportant).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Draft the specification and claims with precision and distinctness. Overbroad or imprecise summaries that claim non-novel matter can vitiate the entire patent. The specification should 'fully explain the principle and the several modes' of application.

rubrics_metrics.name: Requirement to disclose the principle and several modes
rubrics_metrics.description: A clause in the Patent Acts requires that the inventor in his specification 'fully explain the principle and the several modes, in which he has contemplated the application of that principle or character, by which it may be distinguished from other inventions.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Include full explanation of the inventive principle and the different modes of applying it; this both enables unity claims for multiple modes and supports enforceability. Use the specification to show alternatives and modes that the inventor contemplates as part of the single invention.

rubrics_metrics.name: Joint versus sole invention and proper claiming
rubrics_metrics.description: An invention must be claimed as the sole invention of one party if that is the fact, or as the joint invention of two or more parties if it was invented by more than one. A joint invention may be patented, but if a party who was not sole takes the oath declaring himself to be the original and first inventor, the patent will be void.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ensure correct inventorship attribution and oaths; mischaracterizing inventorship risks invalidating patents. Joint patents cannot be consistent with earlier sole patents for the same invention by the same parties.

rubrics_metrics.name: Estoppel: no two subsisting patents for the same invention
rubrics_metrics.description: An inventor cannot have two subsisting valid patents at the same time for the same invention; the first patent, while in force, operates as an estoppel to any subsequent patent by the same person for the same invention.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid taking redundant patents for the same invention and be aware that grant of an initial patent prevents valid later patents for the identical invention by the same inventor. This affects prosecution strategy and assignment/surrender planning.

rubrics_metrics.name: Voidness risk when patent includes non-original claimed matter
rubrics_metrics.description: If a patent covers particulars claimed as the inventor's and any such claimed part is found not to be his invention (i.e., not new), the patent is void; the inclusion of non-original matter in the patent can render it invalid in its entirety unless statute remedies apply for inadvertent mistakes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Claims must avoid including matters not original to the patentee. The Act of 1837 provides limited relief where, by mistake or inadvertence, a patentee claims material not his own, allowing validity for so much as is truly his only if it is material and definitely distinguishable. Nevertheless, careful claim drafting and prior-art searches are crucial.
